originalTitle: ICE detainees in Georgia used the facility’s video calling software to expose the conditions inside
summary: Four men detained at an ICE detention center in rural Georgia used the facility's video conferencing software to expose both the conditions inside and President Donald Trump's hostile takeover of the immigration courts. content: Four men detained at an ICE detention center in rural Georgia used the facility’s video conferencing software to expose both the conditions inside and President Donald Trump’s hostile takeover of the immigration courts. In the five-minute video, the men describe an intentionally dysfunctional legal system designed to keep them trapped in federal custody for months or years — in privately owned facilities that profit from their confinement. The video cost the men, literally and figuratively. The Folkston ICE Processing Center has a work program for detainees in which they are paid a pittance to cook, do laundry, or clean. These wages allow them to buy supplementary food in Folkston’s commissary and stay connected to people outside. “The workers here are paid $1 a day, which is just enough for a 10-minute phone call,” said Idris Makhmudov, one of the men in the video, who says he has been detained in Folkston for 27 months and counting. Makhmudov and the three other men, who are from several different countries, appear in drab, facility-issued uniforms. Their images are blurred by the low-resolution cameras on the detention center’s tablets. It’s unclear exactly how the men made the video, but it’s possible that they called someone on the outside who recorded their message to the outside world. Samantha Hamilton, an Atlanta-based immigration attorney with Asian Americans Advancing Justice, said she received a YouTube link to the video via a Signal chat. “We’ve learned that everyone in the video that was released this weekend has been put into segregation,” said Hamilton, a member of the Shut Down Folkston campaign. “They’re facing retaliation, and they were expecting that.” Since then, 45 detainees wrote an open letter further detailing the conditions at Folkston, and an estimated 73 detainees are now on a hunger strike. [Media: https://twitter.com/EricLeeAtty/status/2107452481202430038] ICE detention isn’t supposed to be a form of punishment; its purpose is ostensibly to ensure that people in deportation proceedings show up to their hearings. But ICE facilities are virtually indistinguishable from prisons — a point the men in the video make repeatedly. Folkston, in fact, was a prison before it became an immigrant detention center. It has many of the hallmarks of prison life, including expensive communication tools that detainees are forced to rely on to talk to people on the outside. “These facilities leave people with very few options to be able to communicate with their loved ones,” said Hamilton, who has had several clients detained at Folkston. She said each “pod” of 60 to 70 detainees has access to just three or four tablets, their only connection to the outside world. Those communications come at a price. To send messages, share photos, or make phone or video calls to their loved ones, detainees at Folkston have to use GettingOut, a proprietary software owned by the prison communications company Telmate. Earlier this year, Telmate was ordered to pay $4.23 million to settle a lawsuit stemming from a 2020 data breach in which users’ information — including names, payment details, and social security numbers — was accessed. Telmate is owned by ViaPath Technologies — formerly GlobalTel*Link — which is in turn owned by American Securities, a New York City-based private equity firm. In 2021, ViaPath charged users anywhere between 18 cents to $1.10 per minute, according to data obtained by the Prison Policy Initiative. These fees add up — so much so that in 2024, the Federal Communications Commission capped the rates companies could charge inmates and detainees to 11 to 25 cents per minute depending on the size of the facility. In 2025, after Trump returned to office, the FCC voted to raise the rate cap by up to 83 percent. Detainees in ICE custody often struggle to get the money they’ve put into these systems back after being released — or, more commonly, deported. GettingOut’s terms of service state that users will lose access to their accounts after 180 days of inactivity, after which they forfeit any money deposited into their accounts. The only way to get their money back is by calling a hard-to-reach customer service line, according to a report by WVTF. Under President Joe Biden, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Tel*Link to pay $3 million for illegally freezing and draining funds from incarcerated people’s accounts. Communications are just one way private companies make money from immigrant detention. Folkston is owned and operated by GEO Group, a publicly traded company whose stock price soared after Trump’s reelection, jumping by more than 75 percent after election day 2024. GEO has donated lavishly to Trump’s campaigns and to related political efforts, contributing $1.4 million to Trump’s super PAC in July — perhaps to show its gratitude for the $165 million it received earlier this year in government contracts. The company receives more than $1.5 million a month to run Folkston, according to a 2021 Homeland Security budget overview. The facility, which has a capacity of 780, has a guaranteed minimum occupancy of 544. Trump’s mass deportation effort, coupled with the backlogged immigration court system, has made it easy for ICE to meet its contractually agreed-upon minimum at Folkston. The men in the video allege that they and others have been there for several years, and explain that the only ways to get out are to be granted parole, bond, or asylum — or to be deported. The latter option is the likeliest now, as Trump has transformed the immigration legal system into what one detainee calls “deportation courts.” Of the 143,729 detained cases logged into Georgia immigration courts over the past year, 81 percent involved people who had no legal representation, and were therefore far less likely to be granted any form of relief, according to federal data analyzed by researchers at Syracuse University. chineseContent: 被拘留在佐治亚州农村地区 ICE 拘留中心的四名男子使用该设施的视频会议软件揭露了内部条件以及唐纳德·特朗普总统对移民法院的敌意接管。在这段五分钟的视频中，这些人描述了一个故意功能失调的法律体系，旨在将他们困在联邦拘留中数月或数年——在从他们的监禁中获利的私人设施中。这段视频让这些人付出了代价，无论是字面上还是象征上。福克斯顿 ICE 处理中心为被拘留者制定了一项工作计划，他们的做饭、洗衣或清洁工作的报酬微薄。这些工资让他们可以在福克斯顿的小卖部购买补充食品，并与外面的人保持联系。视频中的其中一名男子伊德里斯·马赫穆多夫 (Idris Makhmudov) 说：“这里的工人每天工资 1 美元，只够打 10 分钟的电话。”他说，他已在福克斯顿被拘留了 27 个月，而且还在继续。马赫穆多夫和另外三名男子来自几个不同的国家，他们穿着设施配发的土褐色制服。看守所平板电脑上的低分辨率摄像头使他们的图像变得模糊。目前还不清楚这些人到底是如何制作这段视频的，但有可能他们给外部的某个人打电话，而这个人向外界记录了他们的信息。亚裔美国人促进正义组织驻亚特兰大的移民律师萨曼莎·汉密尔顿 (Samantha Hamilton) 表示，她通过 Signal 聊天收到了该视频的 YouTube 链接。 “我们了解到，本周末发布的视频中的每个人都已被隔离，”关闭福克斯顿运动的成员汉密尔顿说。 “他们面临报复，他们也在预料之中。”此后，45 名被拘留者写了一封公开信，进一步详细说明了福克斯顿的条件，并
